resources.string: In recursive descent in C, each rule becomes a function. expr calls termo, and the while repeats as long as a plus comes.
Let's run two times, open paren, three plus four, close paren. expr calls termo, and termo calls fator.
The rule taken literally
A common mistake is copying the rule E, E plus T, as it is. Then expr calls itself before reading any token.
What happens when this expr runs two plus three? Tap it.
Reads the 2 and stops at +
The stack grows until it overflows
Works the same as the while
Before calling expr again, does it read any token?
Each expr calls another expr without reading anything. The input doesn't move, and the stack overflows. That's why the Temple removes left recursion.
op holds the operator, val holds the number, and nome holds the variable. esq and dir are pointers to the children.
Without e =
A common mistake is forgetting the e equals on the novo line. See what comes out with another sum: one plus two plus three.
If the line does not keep the node in e, which tree does expr return? Tap it.
At the end, expr returns e. Where does e point?
The plus node is born, but nobody keeps its address. e stays on leaf 1. With e equals, you get one plus two, plus three.
For two plus three times four, the parser creates the nodes from the bottom up. First the leaves, then the times.
main calls yyparse, the parser Bison wrote. Whenever it needs a token, the parser calls yylex.
Bison and Flex write C files, and gcc puts it all together. Run calc, type the math, and out comes the result.
Without %left
A common mistake is forgetting the %left lines. Bison warns about the shift-reduce conflicts and chooses to shift.
calc.y: %1$s shift/reduce conflicts
Without %left, what does two times three plus four give? Tap it.
It doesn't compile
A conflict is only a warning. When Bison shifts the plus, which operation is left for the end?
Shifting, Bison reduces the plus first: three plus four, seven. Then two times seven, fourteen. With %left, the times comes first and gives ten.
